title: Impossible to miss
core: All of these say a thing is in plain view — no digging, no inference, no benefit of the doubt. The split that matters is what the visibility is *about*: some words only report that something is showing (a fact, a manner, an object), while others add a verdict — that what's showing is a wrong, and that its being unhidden makes it worse. A second split runs underneath: whether concealment was ever an option. Words that presuppose a cover-up carry a charge the purely descriptive ones don't.

words.nuance: The only member that also works as a verb, and that verb defines it: something previously hidden — a disease, a talent, a grudge — surfaces into perception. As an adjective it's the judge's and clinician's word for a fact so evident to the senses that arguing is embarrassing, and it's the one word here that attaches happily to neutral or good things (manifest talent, manifest destiny).

Reserve it for **claims**, not acts or objects: a patent lie, patent nonsense, a patent absurdity. It's the only one that reliably tells you the speaker is exasperated — the fact was lying wide open and someone had the nerve to pretend otherwise.

Describes the **manner** of doing, not the plainness of a fact, and it only earns its keep when hiding was the expected move — it's the live antonym of *covert*. Overt hostility means the pretending has stopped; an overt act of war means the openness is the message.

The eye's word, not the mind's: the thing juts out of its surroundings and pulls attention, regardless of truth or wrongdoing. It's the only one that comfortably describes a person, a garment, or a *gap* — conspicuous by his absence — and the only one that can slide into vulgarity (conspicuous consumption) rather than condemnation.

Adds moral heat and demands a rule to break: a flagrant violation, breach, abuse, disregard. What it condemns is the **shamelessness** — the offender didn't even bother to hide — so it's the one word here that says something about the offender's attitude rather than about how easy the thing is to see.

The only one measuring **degree of badness** rather than degree of exposure — outstandingly bad, worst-of-its-kind. An egregious error can be quietly buried and only discovered later; it stays egregious. Say it about a small private slip and you sound ridiculous.

exam_note: Sentence Equivalence baits you with a pair of condemning words (flagrant/egregious) when the sentence only supports visibility (manifest/conspicuous) — check whether the blank needs a wrong, or just a thing that shows.
